title: Returns and volatility from NSE data
summary: Load ten years of daily prices for a few Nifty stocks and the index, and turn them into the numbers every analysis starts from: returns, rolling volatility, drawdowns and correlations.
data: NSE's daily bhavcopy archive, or a library such as yfinance with .NS tickers
Prices adjusted for splits, bonuses and dividends
steps: Load daily closes for Nifty 50 and five large stocks, and check for gaps, zeros and duplicate dates
Adjust for splits and bonuses, and confirm no day shows a fake −50% move
Compute simple and log daily returns, and check that log returns add up to the total
Compute 20-day and 60-day rolling volatility, annualised with √252, and plot them
Compute the drawdown series and the maximum drawdown for each stock and the index
Compute the correlation matrix of daily returns, then again only on the 20 worst Nifty days
Write three findings in plain sentences, each with the number behind it
deliverable: A notebook with the charts, and the three findings at the top.
stretch: Compare realised vol with India VIX over the same dates
Check whether volatility clusters: is a big day more likely after a big day?

review.q: A stock's daily returns have a standard deviation of 1.5%. What is its annualised volatility?
options: About 24%
About 378%
About 1.5%
About 9%

review.q: One day shows a −50% return in an otherwise calm stock. What is the first thing to check?
options: A 1:2 split or bonus the prices aren't adjusted for
Whether the stock was in the news that week or month
Whether the 20-day volatility window is too short
Whether to drop the stock from the study altogether
review.why: Unadjusted corporate actions are the usual cause of fake crashes. Fix the data before reading anything into it.

review.q: Correlations between your stocks are much higher on the 20 worst Nifty days. What does that mean for a portfolio?
options: Diversification works least when it's needed most
The stocks are bad hedges in calm markets
Volatility is lower on bad days
The correlation estimate is wrong and should be ignored
review.why: Correlations rise in sell-offs, so a portfolio that looks diversified on average can fall together in a crash.

review.q: Why use log returns when adding up returns over time?
options: Log returns add up across days; simple returns compound
Log returns are always smaller, so they're safer
Simple returns can't be negative
Log returns remove the need to adjust prices
review.why: The sum of daily log returns is the log of the total growth, so they aggregate cleanly over time.

title: A momentum backtest with costs
summary: Test a 12-month momentum strategy on Nifty 100 stocks, rebalanced monthly, with honest costs and a clean out-of-sample period. This is the classic first research project.
data: Monthly adjusted prices for the Nifty 100, with the members as of each date
Brokerage, STT and an impact estimate for costs
steps: Write the hypothesis and the rules before touching the data, and set aside the last three years as out of sample
Build the universe as of each month-end, so stocks that later dropped out are included
Rank stocks on 12-month return skipping the last month, and form a top-decile portfolio
Lag the signal so each month's portfolio uses only data known at the previous month-end
Charge costs on every trade: brokerage, STT both ways and about 10 bps of impact
Report CAGR, Sharpe, maximum drawdown, turnover and hit rate, gross and net of costs
Run the untouched out-of-sample period once, and compare it with the in-sample results
Regress the returns on the Nifty to split out beta and alpha
deliverable: A notebook and a one-page summary: the rules, the gross and net results, and whether it survives costs out of sample.
stretch: Test sensitivity: 6, 9 and 12-month lookbacks, and quintiles instead of deciles
Add a crash filter and see whether it helps out of sample, not just in sample

review.q: Your backtest uses today's Nifty 100 members back to 2012. What does that do to the results?
options: It flatters them: stocks that crashed out of the index are missing
It hurts them, because newer index members are left out entirely
Nothing changes, as long as all the prices are split-adjusted
It only changes volatility and drawdowns, not the average return
review.why: That's survivorship bias: the stocks that crashed out of the index are exactly the ones a momentum book might have held.

review.q: Gross Sharpe is 1.2 and net Sharpe is 0.3. What does that point to?
options: High turnover: costs eat most of the edge
The out-of-sample period is far too short
The signal must have look-ahead bias in it
The strategy needs more leverage to work
review.why: A big gap between gross and net is a cost problem. Look at turnover and whether slower rebalancing keeps the edge.

review.q: Why skip the most recent month when measuring 12-month momentum?
options: Last-month returns tend to reverse, which fights the signal
The latest month's prices aren't published until later
It makes the backtest run faster on large universes
Exchange rules require a one-month lag on any signal
review.why: One-month returns show short-term reversal, so the standard momentum signal is 12-month return minus the last month.

review.q: You tried 40 variants in sample and picked the best. How should you read its Sharpe?
options: As an overestimate: the best of many tries is partly luck
As the expected live Sharpe
As an underestimate, because costs were included
As meaningless, since backtests can't be trusted
review.why: Selecting the best of many trials inflates performance. Expect less, and judge it on the untouched out-of-sample period.

title: A pairs trade that might break
summary: Find two related stocks, test whether their spread mean-reverts, and trade it with entry, exit and stop rules. Then see what happens when the relationship breaks.
data: Daily adjusted prices for candidate pairs in one sector, such as two private banks or two cement makers
Single-stock futures margins and lot sizes for the costs and shorting
steps: Pick five candidate pairs on economic grounds, before looking at any charts
Estimate the hedge ratio with a regression on a formation period only
Test the spread for cointegration (Engle-Granger or ADF) and estimate its half-life
Set rules: enter at a z-score of ±2, exit near 0, stop at ±4, using rolling statistics
Backtest on the next period with costs, and record every trade
Find a period where the pair broke, and explain what changed in the business
Report hit rate, average win and loss, holding period and worst trade
deliverable: A notebook with the test results, the trade list and a paragraph on the break.
stretch: Re-estimate the hedge ratio every quarter and compare
Run the same rules on 20 pairs and see how many survive

review.q: Two stocks are highly correlated but not cointegrated. What does that mean for a pairs trade?
options: The spread can drift away for good, so reversion isn't assured
The trade is safer than one on a cointegrated pair would be
The hedge ratio between the two must be exactly one
They will always move together, so the spread never moves
review.why: Correlation is about daily moves; cointegration is about the spread returning to a mean. Only the second supports a pairs trade.

review.q: The spread's half-life is 60 trading days. What does that tell you?
options: Trades take months to revert, so costs and break risk add up
The spread usually reverts within a few trading days
The pair is not cointegrated, so the test was wrong
You should enter at a z-score of 1 rather than 2
review.why: A long half-life means slow convergence, so capital is tied up and costs and the risk of a break build up.

review.q: Why set a stop at a z-score of 4?
options: A spread that keeps widening may mean the pair has broken
To lock in profits on the trades that are winning
Because the exchange requires a stop on all pairs
To cut brokerage on trades that stay open a while
review.why: Mean reversion strategies lose most when the relationship stops holding. A stop caps the damage from a break.

review.q: You estimated the hedge ratio and z-score on the full sample. What's wrong?
options: It uses future data, so the backtest has look-ahead
Nothing: more data always gives better estimates
It makes the half-life come out far too short
The z-score should use the median, not the mean
review.why: Statistics must come from data available at the time: a formation period, then rolling estimates.

title: A Black-Scholes pricer checked against the market
summary: Write a Black-Scholes pricer with Greeks, solve for implied volatility, and check it against the live Nifty option chain. Then plot the smile the model can't explain.
data: The Nifty option chain from the NSE website, saved at one time of day
Nifty spot or futures at the same time, and a risk-free rate such as the T-bill yield
steps: Code the call and put prices, and check put-call parity holds to a few paise
Code delta, gamma, vega and theta, and check each against a small bump of the input
Write an implied-volatility solver (Newton or bisection) and test it on prices you generated
Download one expiry's chain and back out implied vol at every strike with enough volume
Plot implied vol against strike: the smile, or skew
Compare the at-the-money straddle price with the implied move it gives
Note where the model and the market disagree, and why traders accept it
deliverable: A notebook with the pricer, tests and the smile chart.
stretch: Use the Nifty future instead of spot to avoid guessing the dividend yield
Repeat across three expiries and plot the term structure

review.q: Your call price and put price break put-call parity by ₹40. What is most likely wrong?
options: A bug in the pricer, or mismatched rate or time inputs
The market is offering free money on this expiry
Black-Scholes doesn't apply to puts, only calls
The option chain was delayed when you saved it
review.why: Parity follows from no-arbitrage alone. A big break in your own model's prices means a coding or input error.

review.q: Out-of-the-money puts show higher implied vol than out-of-the-money calls. What is this called?
options: Skew: traders pay up for downside protection
Term structure: far expiries cost more
Vol crush: implied vol falls after events
Gamma risk: delta moves fast near expiry
review.why: In equity indices, demand for crash protection lifts the implied vol of low strikes: the skew.

review.q: How do you check that your vega is coded right?
options: Bump vol by 1 point, reprice, and compare with vega
Check that vega always comes out as a positive number
Compare it with delta at the same strike and expiry
Make sure vega stays below 1 for every strike shown
review.why: A finite-difference bump is the standard check for any Greek.

review.q: Why might you price off the Nifty future rather than spot?
options: The future already prices in carry and dividends, so fewer guesses
Spot isn't published during market hours, only at the close
Futures have no expiry, so time to expiry drops out
Black-Scholes only works with futures, never with spot
review.why: Using the forward (Black's model) avoids estimating dividends and the exact carry.

title: An execution simulator
summary: Simulate working a large buy order against an intraday volume curve. Compare VWAP-style, front-loaded and fixed-rate schedules on cost and risk.
data: Average intraday volume by 15 or 30-minute bucket for a liquid stock
A simple impact model, such as cost in bps proportional to the square root of participation
steps: Build the stock's average volume profile across the day from historical data
Simulate price paths with realistic intraday volatility
Code three schedules: follow the volume profile, front-load, and a fixed participation rate
Add temporary impact per slice and permanent impact that lifts later prices
Measure each schedule against VWAP and against the arrival price
Run a thousand days and compare the average cost and the spread of outcomes
Explain the trade-off between impact and timing risk you see
deliverable: A notebook with the simulator and a chart of average cost against risk for each schedule.
stretch: Add a participation cap and see which schedules fail to finish
Fit the impact coefficient to real fills if you can get them

review.q: Front-loading beats VWAP on average in your simulator. Why might that be?
options: Your own buying lifts later prices, which raises the VWAP benchmark
Front-loading always has lower impact than any other schedule
The volume profile is wrong, so VWAP is mismeasured
VWAP ignores the opening auction, where front-loaders buy
review.why: When your own buying moves the price, early fills look cheap against a VWAP your later trades pushed up. Check against arrival too.

review.q: Trading faster cuts timing risk but costs what?
options: More market impact per share
More timing risk
Lower participation
Nothing; faster is always better
review.why: That's the core trade-off Almgren-Chriss formalises: impact against the risk of prices moving while you wait.

review.q: Why measure against the arrival price as well as VWAP?
options: VWAP can hide the cost of the market moving while you traded
The arrival price is always lower than VWAP on a buy
VWAP is not a benchmark used by Indian brokers
Arrival price already includes brokerage and STT
review.why: Implementation shortfall against arrival captures the full cost of the decision to trade, including drift during execution.

review.q: Your fixed 10% rate fails to finish on light days. What would fix it best?
options: Size each slice to what's left over the volume left today
Trade 25% of the volume all day, every day, to be safe
Buy everything at the open, when volume is heaviest
Only trade the order on days with heavy volume
review.why: A pace that adapts to remaining shares and expected volume finishes without breaching a cap.

title: A two-page research note
summary: Write up one of the projects as a desk memo a PM can read in five minutes: the claim, the evidence, the risks and what you'd do next.
data: Your notebook from one of the other projects
steps: Open with the result in two sentences: what you found and how sure you are
State the hypothesis and why it should work, in plain words
Show one chart and one table, no more, each with a sentence saying what to see
Give gross and net numbers, the out-of-sample result and the worst period
List what could make it fail: costs, capacity, crowding, a regime change
Say what you'd test next and what result would make you drop the idea
Ask someone to read it cold, and fix anything they had to ask about
deliverable: Two pages, as a PDF or a doc, written so someone who missed the meeting gets it.
stretch: Present it in two minutes out loud, then take questions
Write the one-paragraph version for an email

review.q: What should the first two sentences of a research note do?
options: Give the result and how confident you are
Describe the data sources
Thank the people who helped
Explain the history of the strategy
review.why: Busy readers decide from the opening whether to read on, so the answer comes first.

review.q: Your in-sample Sharpe is 1.8 and out-of-sample 0.6. What goes in the note?
options: Both, with the out-of-sample one as the honest guide
Only the in-sample number, since it uses more data
Only the out-of-sample number; drop the in-sample one
The average of the two, 1.2, as a fair middle ground
review.why: Hiding the drop costs you credibility. The out-of-sample figure is the better guide to live performance.

review.q: Which belongs in the risks section?
options: Capacity: how much it can run before costs eat the edge
The Python and library versions used for the backtest
How long the backtest took to run on your laptop
Ideas for a completely different strategy to try
review.why: PMs want to know what can go wrong and how big it can get. Capacity and costs are first on that list.

review.q: Why say in advance what result would make you drop the idea?
options: It stops you moving the goalposts after the data
It's required by SEBI for every research note
It makes the note shorter and easier to read
It helps the strategy pass its review first time
review.why: Committing to a kill criterion in advance is a guard against data snooping and wishful thinking.
